name: Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale
title: Pattern 10: Pilot Small, Measure, Then Scale
answer: Pattern 10 says a school should test an AI tool with a small group of teachers for a set time, measure one meaningful result, and then decide to expand, adjust, or stop. It matters because stopping a tool that did not work is a success, since it prevents a mistake from spreading to every classroom. The pattern is meant to be used before any of the other nine patterns reaches all classrooms.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern is about how a school adopts any of the other nine ideas. Rather than buying a tool for every classroom at once, the school runs a short trial with a few teachers. The trial measures one thing that matters and ends with a clear decision. The decision can be to expand, to adjust, or to stop. Stopping is treated as a success when the tool did not work, because it keeps the district from spreading a mistake.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: A good pilot is short and specific. It names two or three teachers, one measure such as minutes saved or a skill score, a starting baseline, and a date for the decision meeting. The text does not give grade bands for this pattern, so it is described as a school level adoption method rather than a classroom activity for a particular age group. Figure 2.7 shows the shape, and Chapter 4 turns it into a full template. Every idea in the Volume should pass through a pilot like this before it reaches every classroom.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this as research and gives two reasons for caution. First, realistic effects are small, and short trials often show no learning gain even when students like the tool. In one randomized trial, students using AI scored higher on exercises but learned no more than students without it, and they preferred the tool that helped them least (Bassner et al., 2026). Second, promised time savings often fail to appear, and a review of automatic feedback found that nearly half the studies showed no reduction in instructor workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that a pilot can show no learning gain even when students enjoy the tool, and that expected time savings may not appear. The text also warns that realistic effects are small, so a short trial may not prove a learning benefit. The decisions to expand, adjust, or stop stay with the school and are made at a set decision meeting. Stopping is not a failure when the tool did not work, because it protects the district from spreading a mistake. The pattern does not remove human judgment, it structures when that judgment is made.
